Full-fledged banking functions by Postal Department 
*321. SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRASEKHAR: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state:  
(a) whether the Department of Posts has approached RBI to  grant it licence to 
convert its Savings Account into a full-fledged bank; 
(b) if so, the number of its branches in the country, which would perform such 
functions, State-wise; 
(c) whether the staff deputed for performing full -fledged banking duties would be 
paid suitable scales as given to the staff in the public sector banks; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY 
(SHRI A. RAJA): (a) No, Sir. The Department of Posts has not approached the Reserve 
Bank of India to grant it license to convert the Post Office Savings Bank (POSB) in to a 
full-fledged bank as the POSB is an agency function carried out by the Department of 
Posts on behalf of the Ministry of Finance under the provisions of Government Savings 
Bank Act, 1873. 
(b) to (d) Do not arise in view of (a) above.

MoU for legal migration 
*323.    SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: 
DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA A. HEPTULLA: 
Will the Minister of OVERSEAS INDIAN AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether his Ministry and the International Organization for Migration signed a 
Memorandum of Unders tanding for the project ‘‘Regional Dialogue and Facilitating 
Managed and Legal Migration between Asia and the European Union’’; 
(b) if so, the details of this scheme; 
 
(c) in what manner this would be helpful in reducing illegal migration to European 
countries; 
(d) the modalities of legal help to be given to migrant workers; and 
(e) to what extent European Union has responded to management of  
immigration in their own countries? 
THE MINISTER OF OVERSEAS INDIAN AFFAIRS (SHRI VAYALAR RAVI): 
(a) to (e) A Memorandum of Unde rstanding (MoU) has been signed between the 
Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs (MOIA) and the International Organisation for 
Migration (IOM) for implementation of the project ‘‘Regional Dialogue and 
Programme on Facilitating Managed and Legal Migration between Asia and the 
European Union (EU)’’. 
The project is sponsored by European Union (EU) and covers 10 Asian countries 
(Bangladesh, China, India, Indonesia, Nepal, Pakistan, Philippines, Sri Lanka, Thailand, 
Vietnam; for some activities Afghanistan) and 5  European countries (Germany, Ireland, 
Italy, Spain and U.K). 
The project is aimed at facilitating development of legal migration, enhancing 
regional cooperation on legal migration management, reducing irregular migration, 
enhancing placement capacity amon gst recruiting agencies and dissemination of 
information relating to employment opportunities and procedures to intending 
emigrants. 
The project will seek to promote and facilitate legal migration of Indian workers to 
the European Union through a wide range of activities including training at the 

6       Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Starred Questions 
national level for the potential workers and recruiters, preparation of a national 
manpower profile for overseas deployment, enhancing the quality of tech nical training 
and certification, establishing a model migrants resource centre to provide information 
to potential Emigrant workers and an information campaign to create awareness among 
potential migrant workers on the risks of illegal migration. 
The Project also envisages a pilot placement programme between India and the five 
participating EU countries. 
As present, the vast majority of the semi -skilled/skilled workers from India go to the 
Gulf countries for employment. This project will help diversify Ind ia’s overseas 
employment destination base to a region where considerable employment opportunities 
are expected to emerge in the ensuing years. 
The Ministry has been taking several measures to address the problem of illegal 
migration including introducing e -governance, revamping the recruiting agency system, 
liberalization of the migration policy regime etc. This project will be a part of the 
Government’s efforts to reduce illegal migration to the European Union and facilitate 
legal migration. It is expected  that in the medium to long term all these measures will 
help and reduce the problem of illegal migration from India. 
Allotment of Janta flats in Narela 
*324. SHRI RAJ NATH SINGH: Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state; 
(a) whether Government are aware of the huge delay in completion of paper work 
and other formalities in the allotment of Janta flats in Narela and other areas under DDA 
1996 Scheme; 
(b) whether the allottees are yet to be given possession in several cases; 
(c) whether despite submiss ion of all documents, allotment of flats in Sector A -6, 
Pocket-II remains to be done as DDA is yet to issue a conveyance deed; 
(d) by when these allotments are likely to be made; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI S. JAIP AL REDDY): (a) 
The Delhi Development Authority (DDA) has reported that there is no delay in 
completion of paper work and other formalities in allotment of Janta flats in Narela and 
other areas under DDA. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) DDA has further reported that the conv eyance deed papers have been issued in 
cases, where payments, along with the prescribed documents, have been submitted by 
the allottees. 
(d) and (e) DDA has further reported that allotments have been made to 18347 out 
of 20,000 registrants and there is a backl og of only 709 registrants under the scheme. 
DDA has prepared an action plan for allotment of flats to these wait -listed registrants by 
September, 2007.

Recommendations of T.L. Shankar Committee 
*325.    SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a Parliamentary Committee has criticized the Ministry for failing to 
ensure development of captive coal blocks by the allocattees and demanded  that such 
blocks be de-allocated if they continued to remain unutilized; 
(b) if so, the other recommendations made by the Committee; 
(c) whether an experts’ Committee headed by T.L. Shankar had submitted the 
second part of the report to the Centre on coal sector reforms; 
(d) whether Government have accepted the recommendations; and 
(e) the steps being taken to implement them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. DASARI 
NARAYANA, RAO): (a) The Standing Committee on Coal and Steel had observed in 
their 23rd re port on Demand for Grants (2007- 08) that some of the coal blocks allotted 
as early as 1998 to 2000 have still not been developed and only 8 blocks have started 
producing coal. The Ministry of Coal in its reply to the Committee had, inter -alia, 
stated that out of the 19 coal blocks allotted up to 2002, 11 have already come into 
production and 6 more are expected to commence production during 2007- 08. The 
Committee was further informed that the position has since improved on account of 
measures taken by the M inistry such as intensive monitoring being done on a regular 
basis, prescription of time -bound milestones, introduction of bank guarantee deposit 
system etc. 
(b) The Committee had, inter-alia, recommended as below: 
(i)   Simplification of procedure for allocation of coal blocks and 
facilitation of various approvals such as previous approval by the 
Central Government and grant of mining lease by State Government. 
(ii)  Coal Controller’s Office should be strengthened adequately so that 
they could monitor the progress as provided under the rules and take 
corrective steps. 
(iii)  Issue of notice to both public and private companies asking them to 
develop the coal blocks within a stipulated time failing which the coal 
blocks allocated to them would be de-allocated. 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) and (e) Do not arise in view of the answer given to part (c) of the  
question.

Security assistance to Pakistan 
*327.    SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether according to a study by the US experts Pakistan has received $ 1.8 
billion as security assistance from US for the war against terrorism, but the weapons 
financed under it are more useful in countering India than fighting Al Qaida and 
Taliban; 

Written Answers to [6 SEP., 2007] Starred Questions       9 
(b) whether US has recommended that the billions of dollars given to Pakistan in aid 
to fight terrorism be tied to its performance; 
(c) whether India has always been urging USA not to provide funds to  Pakistan as 
they are used against India; and 
(d) if so, to what extent India’s stand has been proved by this study report? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): (a) 
According to a study conducted by Craig Cohen and Derek Chollet of Center for 
Strategic and International Studies, a Washington based think -tank, out of the $10 
billion of assistance provided by US to Pakistan over the past five -plus years, roughly 
18 per cent or $1.8 billion has gone toward security assistance. According to thi s report, 
this assistance is often justified as playing a critical role in the war on terrorism, 
whereas, in reality, the weapons systems are often ‘prestige items’ to help Pakistan in 
the event of war with India. The study emphasises that few of these weapons are likely 
to provide much help in rooting out Al Qaeda or the Taliban. 
(b) The 'Implementing Recommendations of the 9/11 Commission Act of 2007' 
signed into law by President Bush on August 3, 2007 has prescribed limitations on US 
security assistance to P akistan for FY 2008. The Act states that authorisation for 
appropriations for subsequent fiscal years shall be determined by the extent to which the 
Government of Pakistan displays demonstrable progress, inter alia , in ‘‘preventing Al 
Qaeda and other terro rist organizations from operating in the territory of Pakistan, 
including eliminating terrorist camps or facilities, arresting members and leaders of 
terrorist organizations, and countering recruitment efforts’’. 
(c) and (d) Government of lndia’s position in t his regard is well known. We are 
against an arms race in our region. Government's concerns have been expressed to the 
US and other nations. Government will take all necessary steps to safeguard India’s 
security.

PRIs to implement Centrally sponsored schemes 
*334. SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of PANCHAYATI RAJ be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the third meeting of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj had proposed to 
make Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) play a key role in implementing the Centrally 
sponsored schemes; 
(b) if so, whether the Competent Authority has approved the above proposal; 
(c) if so, the details including steps taken/to be taken to implement the same; 
(d) the details of steps taken/to be taken to identify such Centrally sponsored 
schemes as on today; and 
(e) the details of the steps taken by State Governments in mainstreaming local self -
Government institutions by devolving power and funds, State-wise and category-wise as 
on date? 
THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ (SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) 
to (d) Yes, Sir. A key priori ty of the Ministry of Pachayati Raj is to critically examine 
major Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSSs) to ensure that in the design, articulation of 
their guidelines, and subsequently in implementation, the operationalizing of CSSs do 
not overlook the salie nce of Panchayats and Gram Sabhas. In September, 2004, the 
Prime Minister’s Office approved a suggestion from the Ministry of Panchayati Raj that 
all Ministries operating CSSs should review their respective schemes in the light of the 
73rd Constitutional Amendment, so that they are in consonance with Article 243 G read 
with Eleventh Schedule of the Constitution. The Eleventh Schedule has an illustrative 
listing of 29 matters that every State Government ought to devolve to Panchayats. It was 
further approved that the Ministry of Panchayati Raj should be consulted and its views 
incorporated in Notes prepared for Cabinet Committees, in respect of new Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes. Accordingly, The Ministry of Panchayati Raj has been in dialogue 
with Central Government Ministries over 2005 and 2006, and some modifications have 
been incorporated in some of the Centrally Sponsored Schemes. The Cabinet Secretary 
has repeatedly reminded Central Government Ministries of their responsibility towards 
incorporating appropriate modifications. However, the response pattern was not always 
sufficiently brisk. 
In order to further galvanize this process, and at the request of the Minister for 
Panchayati Raj, Youth Affairs, Sports, and DONER, a Review Corrimittee has been  

22     Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Starred Questions 
constituted in the Cabinet Secretariat with Secretary (Coordination and Public 
Grievances) and Secretary (Panchayati Raj) as Co -Chairs. This Review Committee has 
commenced its meetings on 17 August, 2007, and has already met with Secretaries of 
nine Central Ministries to determine the extent of centrality being accorded, in letter and 
spirit, in the guidelines issued by the Central Ministries, which determine the processes 
of implementation of the Centrally  Sponsored Scheme. The review is expected to be 
completed by the end of September, 2007. 
At the third meeting of the Council of Ministers of Panchayati Raj convened on 17 -
18 August, 2007 at Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, under the Chairmanship of the Union 
Minister of Panchayati Raj, the Council in its conclusions, stated as follows: 
‘‘The Council of Ministers resolves that since Ministry of Panchayati Raj has been 
meticulously mapping the progress achieved across States, inclusive of the implements 
they are encountering in moving ahead, and there is now an enormous amount of State 
specific data compiled, and further since the dialogue with Central Ministries in respect 
of Centrally Sponsored Schemes is nearing completion through a Committee lodged in 
the Cabinet Secretariat, it would be appropriate that Chairman and Deputy Chairman of 
the Planning Commission be requested to convene a meeting of the National 
Development Council, chaired by Hon’ble Prime Minister on Panchayati Raj and 
Decentralized Planning’’.

Safeguarding interests of labourers 
†*336. SHRI RUDRA NARAYAN PANY: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether private sector companies are also the members of JBCCI set up for coal 
industry; 
(b) whether decision taken in JBCCI are also applicable to these companies; and 
(c) if not, the measures being  taken by Government to safeguard the interests of 
labourers of these private companies? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. DASARI 
NARAYAN RAO): (a) No, Sir. Private Coal Companies have not agreed to be 
associated with the Joint Bipartite Committee for Coal Industry (JBCCI-VIII). 
(b) No, Sir, Since the decisions to be taken in JBCCI -VIII are to be implemented by 
the signatory companies, these would not be applicable to private sector companies, 
who are not participating in the negotiations of JBCCI-VIII. 
(c) As far as private sector companies are concerned, the wage settlement etc., be it 
bipartite or tripartite, are signed when the parties agree to sign the settlement. There is 
no provision to force any party to sign the settlement. However, if the demands placed 
before the employer are not accepted by him, the aggrieved union can always raise an 
industrial dispute before the conciliation machinery. If the dispute is not settled, the 
matter is referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The  interests of labourers 
in private sector companies are safeguarded in accordance with provisions of the 
Minimum Wages Act. Sufficient safeguards have been provided under the above Act 
and relevant Rules with respect to the wages, service conditions, provi dent fund, health 
and other social security measures. Enforcement of the above Act and Rules is the 
responsibility of the concerned State Governments in their jurisdiction.

Joining N-experiment Club 
2451. SHRI RA JKUMAR DHOOT: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India has decided to join N -experiment Club spending 
huge amount of money; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the future plans for production of nuclear power during the next five years and 
the cost of production per unit of nuclear power; and 
(d), the areas likely to be benefitted by this club? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER’S OFFICE (SHRI 
PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) and (b) There are a number of international 
groupings/projects on nuclear related research. India joined International 
Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) as a full partner in 2006 along with the 
European Atomic Energy Community (EURATOM), China, Japan, Republic of Korea, 
Russia and the United States of  America. The salient feature of ITER project is to 
demonstrate the scientific and technological feasibility of fusion energy for peaceful 
purposes, an essential feature of which would be achieving sustained fusion power 
generation. The aim of ITER project  is to show that fusion could be used to generate 
electrical power and to gain the necessary data to design and operate the first electricity 
producing plant. The resources of the ITER organisation shall be from contributions of 
member States in agreed pro portions. The approximate financial implication on the part 
of India is estimated at Rs. 2500 crores over a period of 10 years which will be largely 
in the form of in-kind contribution. 
(c) The present capacity in operation of 4120 MWe is planned to be increas ed to 
7280 MWe in the next five years. Work on eight indigenous PHWRs with a total 
capacity of 5600 MWe and ten Light Water Reactors with a total capacity of 10,000 
MWe based on imports has been proposed to be started in the Eleventh Plan. The 
current average tariff on nuclear power station is about Rs. 2.30. 
(d) India’s joining ITER is recognition of India’s scientific and technological 
capability in fusion energy. Considering India’s large energy needs in future, our 
gaining technological capability in fusion energy will be of considerable long term

2464. SHRI VEDPRAKASH P. GOYAL: Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS

INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) and (b) Sir, TRAI

Fine on Reliance Infocomm by TDSAT 
2466. SHRI KAMAL AKHTAR: Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS AND 
INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact t hat Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal 
(TDSAT) has fined a sum of Rs. 150 crores on Reliance Infocomm for breaching 
license conditions; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMUNICATIONS AND 
INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
TDSAT in its judgment dated 4th March, 2005 dismissed the petition No. 3 of 2005 
filed by M/s Reliance Infocomm Ltd. (RlL) against the orders of Department of 
Telecommunications regarding imposition of penalty of Rs.l50 crores. The details of the 
case are as follows: 
(i)   A complaint was received from VSNL in respect of incorrect Calling Line 
Identity (CLI) for international calls on 2nd June, 2004. Meanwhile similar 
complaints were received from other sources also. 
(ii)  After detailed investigation it was concluded that RIL has tampered with 
CLI and had avoided the payment of Access Deficit Charges, thereby had 
violated the terms and conditions of various Licence Agreements. 
(iii)  Government after following the due process as per provisions of the 
Licence Agreements levied a penalty of Rs.150 crores on M/s RIL (Rs.50 
crores each against the Unified Access Services Licences of Chennai, 
Mumbai and Kolkata service areas). 
(iv)  M/s RIL appealed in the Tel ecom Dispute Settlement and Appellate 
Tribunal (TDSAT), however, the appeal was dismissed. M/s RIL paid the 
penalty of Rs.150 crores in March, 2005. 
(v)   M/s RIL further filed a Civil Appeal in the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India 
against the judgement of the TDSAT and the matter is subjudice.

2495. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state:  
(a) whether Government are aware that the quantity of the carbon dioxide has 
increased tremendously in the atmosphere and as a result thereof the temperature of 
earth has been increasing; 
(b) if so, the quantity thereof so increased during the last three years, year -wise and 
country-wise; and 
(c) the efforts which are being made by Government to reduce this quantity to keep 
the earth in a normal atmosphere? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) According to Fourth 
Assessment Report of the three Working Groups of the Inter -governmental Panel on 
Climate Change, the global atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide has increased 
at the rate of 2.5 parts per million (ppm) by volume per year since the year 2000. The 
atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide during three years, viz. 2005, 2004 and 
2003, were 379 ppm, 376.5 ppm and 374 ppm respectively. The country -wise estimates 
of atmospheric concentration are not recorded. The updated 100 years linear trend of 
increase of average global surface air temperature is 0.74 degree Celsius. 
(c) The Government of India is a Party to the Kyoto Protocol to the United Nations 
Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCCC) and has set up the National 
Clean Development Mechanism Authority to accord Host Country Approvals (HCA) to 
eligible Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) projects. In dia also has the largest 
number of projects under the CDM of the Kyoto Protocol, which reduce net emissions 
of greenhouse gases. 
Further, even though India as a developing country does not have any mitigation 
commitments, nevertheless, a sustainable develo pment path is being followed through a 
range of policies and programmes to mitigate climate change:

Disposing of wastes from Indian industries 
†2497.   SHRI RUDRA NARAYAN PANY: 
SHRI SHREEGOPAL VYAS: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any scheme or recommendation to dispose of the waste of 
India’s industries which is harmful to environment; 
(b) the names of the countries from where such waste is coming to India along with 
the quantity; 
(c) the names of the States which are recycling such waste and to what extent 
success has been achieved in this regard; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

Written Answers to [6 SEP., 2007] Unstarred Questions     99 
(d) whether any treaty has been signed in this regard; and 
(e) the purpose of importing such waste? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) The Ministry of Environment and 
Forests, Government of India have notified the Hazardous Waste (Manage ment and 
Handling) Rules, 1989 as amended in 2000 and 2003 under the Environment 
(Protection) Act, 1986. These rules regulate the collection, storage, transportation, 
treatment, disposal, import and export of hazardous wastes listed in the Schedules 
annexed to these rules. 
As per the provisions under these rules, the industries are required to treat and 
dispose the hazardous waste in an environmentally sound manner. A Central 
Government Scheme has been formulated wherein financial assistance is given for 
setting up of Treatment Storage and Disposal Facilities (TSDFs). Under this scheme, 
the Ministry of Environment and Forests provides a grant to the tune of Rs.2 crores with 
a proportionate contribution from the State Government for setting up of TSDF on a 
Public Private Partnership involving the Central and State Government and a private 
enterprise through Build Operate Own (BOO) principle. 
(b) to (e) The import of hazardous wastes is regulated under rules 11 to 14 of the 
said rules. According to these rules,  any import of hazardous waste into India for 
dumping and disposal is prohibited. Any hazardous waste containing or contaminated 
with the hazardous waste categories listed in Schedule 8 of these rules is also prohibited 
for imports. 
However, imports of haz ardous wastes listed in Schedules 3 and 4 of the Hazardous 
Waste (Management and Handling) Rules as amended in 2003, is permitted into the 
country for recycling and reprocessing only on a case by case basis. These rules may be 
referred in the Ministry of E nvironment and Forests’s website www.envfor.nic.in. The 
import of hazardous waste is also regulated under the Export Import Policy of the 
Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India. 
The recycling and reprocessing of hazardous wastes is allowed to be carried out only 
by the units registered as recyclers with the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) 
and having environmentally sound management facilities for recycling such wastes. The 
registered recyclers recycle both the indigenously- generated as well as the imported 
hazardous waste. The list of registered recyclers is available with the CPCB’s website 
www.cpcb.nic.in. 
The Government of India is a party to the Basel Conve ntion on Control of 
Transboundary Movement of Hazardous Wastes and their disposal which is the 
International Treaty for regulating the transboundary movement of such wastes. The 
Government of India has ratified the same in 1992. The transboundary movement 
(import and export) of hazardous wastes is also regulated under this Convention 
requiring a prior consent in writing from the importing country for handling such waste 
in an environmentally sound manner. These provisions have also been incorporated in 
the Hazardous Waste (Management and Handling) Rules as amended in 2003.

number of lions in the country particularly in Gir forests; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND

by the Central Government for the reserved forests to prevent poaching in these areas.  
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) The measures taken by Government of India to prevent poaching of wildlife 
including lions, inter alia, include the following: 
 
1. The Central Government has enacted the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 
to deal with the issues of wildlife crime. 
2. Stringent penalties are imposed on the offenders for the contravention of 
the provisions of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. 
3. A n etwork of National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries has been set up 
across the country to protect wildlife.

and Project Elephant , to State/UT Governments for the conservation and 
development of wildlife and its habitats. 
6. India is a signatory to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered 
Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) that regulates international trade 
in wildlife and its derivatives. 
7. India has bilateral arrangements with China and Nepal on combating 
wildlife crime. 
In ad dition, the State of Gujarat has also taken the following measures to protect 
wildlife including lions: 
1. Development of wild life habitat to increase the population of wild animals.

created by the State Governments out of their own resources. The capacity utilization of 
the treatment facilities depends upon the operational efficiency achieved by different 
States through uninterrupted power supply and proper operation and main tenance of the 
assets. 
(b) With the pollution abatement works completed so far in both the phases  
under Ganga Action Plan which also involved creation of a sewage treatment  
capacity of 1747 mld., the water quality of the river Ganga has shown improvement  
at major locations over its pre -GAP quality according to the water quality  
monitoring done by independent reputed institutions of the country. In respect of  
river Yamuna, the quality of river water has not shown the desired improvement  
owing to the large ga p between the demand and the availability of sewage  
treatment capacity particularly in Delhi, and the lack of availability of fresh water  
for ensuring minimum flow in the river. The works in respect of other rivers are at  
different stages of completion. 
Conservation of rivers is a dynamic activity with the ever increasing pollution load 
due to increase in population. Review of the strategies of conservation policy and 
identification of additional towns and rivers is a continuous process. Water being a State  
subject, it is the responsibility of State Governments to create proper sewerage 
infrastructure to prevent pollution from entering the rivers. Central Government only 
supplements the efforts of the State Governments by providing one time grant for 
capital works for identified polluted stretches. National River Conservation Plan is a 
major programme of the Government. A total amount of about Rs.2981 crore has been 
spent till March, 2007 towards pollution abatement works in the rivers of the country, 
which includes States’ share in the projects. 
(c) While sanctioning the projects under NRCP, the State Governments and the  
Implementing Agencies are encouraged to recycle and reuse the treated sewage  
wherever possible, in order to reduce the fresh water requirements.

(c) Reasons for tiger decline outside tiger reserves and prote cted areas, and the steps

Statement-I 
The reasons for decline in tiger population outside tiger reserves/protected 
areas 
(i)     Degradation of forest status outside Protected Areas/ Tiger Reserves 
owing to : 
(a) human pressure 
(b) livestock pressure 
(c) ecologically unsustainable land uses 
(ii) Loss of forest quality in terms of prey biomass. 
(iii) Tiger deaths due to poaching. 
(iv) Tiger deaths due to man-animal conflict. 
(v) Fragmentation leading to loss of gene flow from source populations. 
(vi)     Loss of reproduction owing to disturbance on account of heavily used 
infrastructure like highways, etc. 
(vii)     Lack of adequate protection in outside areas. 
(viii)     Insurgency/law and order problems in certain areas. 
Statement-II 
Steps taken by the Government for conservation of wild tigers 
Legal steps 
1. Amendment of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 for providing enabling  
provisions for constitution of the National Tiger Conservation  
Authority and the Tiger and Other Endangered Species Crime Control  
Bureau. The punishment in cases of offence within a tiger reserve has  
been enhanced. The Act also provides for forfeiture of any equipment,  
vehicle or weapon that has been used for committing any wild life offence. 
Administrative steps 
2. Strengthening of anti -poaching activities, including special strategy for 
monsoon patrolling, by providing funding support to Tiger Reserve States, as 
proposed by them, for deployment of anti -poaching squads involving ex -army 
personnel, home guards, apart from workforce comprising of local people, in 
addition to strengthening of communication/wireless facilities. 
3. Constitution of the National Tiger Conservation Authority with effect from 
4.09.2006, for strengthening tiger conservation by, inter alia , ensuring 
normative standards in tiger reserve management, preparation of reserve

specific tiger conservation plan, laying down annual/audit report before 
Parliament, constituting State level Steering Committees under the 
Chairmanship of Chief Ministers and establishment of Tiger Conservation 
Foundation. 
4. Constitution of a multidisciplinary Tiger and Other Endangered Species Crime 
Control Bureau (Wildlife Crime Control Bureau) with effect from 6.6.2007 
comprising of officers from Police, Forest, Customs and other enforcement 
agencies to effectively control illegal trade in wildlife. 
5. In principle approval accorded for declaring eight new Tiger Reserves. 
Financial steps 
6. Financial and technical help is provided to the States under various  
Centrally Sponsored Schemes, viz. Project Tiger and Development of  
National Parks and Sanctuaries for enhancing the capacity and  
infrastructure of the States for providing effective protection to wild  
animals. 
International Cooperation 
7. India has a Memorandum of Understanding with Nepal on controlling trans -
boundary illegal trade in wildlife and conservation, apart from a protocol on 
tiger conservation with China. 
8. A Global Tiger Forum of Tiger Range Countries has been created for 
addressing international issues related to tiger conservation. 
9. During the 14th meeting of the Conference of Parties to CITES, which was 
held from 3rd to 15th June, 2007 at The Hague, India introduced a resoluti on 
along with China, Nepal and the Russian Federation, which contains directions 
to Parties with operations breeding tigers on a commercial scale, for restricting 
such captive populations to a level supportive only to conserving wild tigers. 
The resolution  was adopted with minor amendments. Further, India made an 
intervention appealing to China to phase out tiger farming, and eliminate, 
stockpiles of Asian big cats body parts and derivatives. The importance of 
continuing the ban on trade of body parts of tigers was emphasized.

reserves) primarily for the protection of these birds.

Statement 
Declaration of the World Hindi Conference 
The 8th World Hindi Conference was held from  13-15 July, 2007 in New York. The 
inaugural ceremony of the Conference was held at the United Nations Headquarters. 
Inauguration of the 8th World Hindi Conference for the first time ever in the 
Conference Hall of the United Nations Organisation was a hist oric achievement for 
Hindi lovers all over the world. 
Mr. Ban Ki-Moon, Secretary General of the United Nations addressed the Inaugural 
session of the Conference. This in itself was an important achievement. 
The Conference welcomes the resolve to make Hindi , already a language spoken in 
many countries, an official language of the United Nations as mentioned in the audio -
visual address of the Prime Minister, Dr. Manmohan Singh at the inauguration.  
The conference also welcomes the suggestion made by the Prime Minister that Hindi 
writings of Indians living abroad should also be included in the Hindi syllabus and 
standard Hindi curriculum should be developed for teaching Hindi in other countries.  
The conference also welcomes the call made by the Prime Minister to  develop good 
Hindi software, hardware and search engines in order to make Hindi a powerful 
language of the internet and also the need to honour and respect those engaged in the 
field of Hindi both in India and abroad. 
While welcoming the message of the Pr ime Minister, the conference urges the 
Government of lndia to launch a Government -authorised campaign to mobilize support 
of the majority of the member-nations of the United Nations and take all 

122   Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
possible steps to ensure that Hindi is recognized as one of the official languages of the 
UN. NRI Organisations abroad should also make an effort to get the support of the 
Governments of their respective country. 
In addition, as a result of the discussions and deliberations held during the 8th World 
Hindi Conference, the following is proposed: 
1. In order to popularize teaching of Hindi and Devnagari script, a standardized 
syllabus be prepared for teaching Hindi as a second language and a system be evolved 
to recognise Hindi teachers. 
2. To ensure active and purposeful functioning of the World Hindi Secretariat, 
the Governments of India and Mauritius should extend all possible administrative and 
financial assistance to the Secretariat and should consider setting up  of regional offices 
of the Secretariat in Delhi and in 4 -5 other countries. The Conference calls upon the 
Secretariat to develop a website on ‘‘Viswa Manch Per Hindi’’ in order to popularize 
Hindi. 
3. Simple and good books in Hindi on science, technology and technical 
subjects should be encouraged. Effective measures be taken to popularize information 
technology in Hindi. A system based on universally recognized Unicode be developed 
and made available to all. 
4. Database of foreign universities and schools where  Hindi is taught be 
prepared. A list of Hindi teachers should also be prepared. 
5. The Conference calls upon the Hindi lovers of the world, especially non -
resident Indians and Indian nationals working abroad to assist in promotion and 
propagation of Hindi language and literature abroad. 
6. Arrangement for research scholarship be made for foreign Hindi scholars at 
the Mahatma Gandhi Antarrashtriya Hindi Vishwavidyala, Wardha. 
7. Kendriya Hindi Sansthan should also contribute actively in promotion of 
Hindi abroad and preparation of Hindi syllabus. 
8. Setting up of Hindi chairs in foreign university be considered. 
9. In addition to being a language of literature, Hindi should also be used as a 
language of modem science and commerce. 
10. India should encourage use of Hindi at Nati onal and International level 
symposia and conferences.

THE MINISTER OF OVERSEAS INDIAN AFFAIRS (SHRI VAYALAR RAVI): (a) 
and (c) Yes, Sir. The Ministry of Overseas Indian Affai rs has launched a scheme for 
giving legal/financial assistance to women deserted/divorced by their overseas Indian

Statement 
Scheme for giving legal/financial assistance to women deserted by their                     
overseas Indian spouses. 
Objective: 
The objective of the scheme is to provide some financial assistance to needy women 
in d istress who have been deserted by, their overseas Indian spouses for obtaining 
counselling and legal services, The term ‘‘Overseas Indian’’ would include NRls and 
foreign citizens of Indian origin, The counselling and legal services would be provided 
through credible Indian Women’s Organizations/ Indian Community Associations and 
NGOs identified for providing such services and empanelled with the Indian Missions 
in the USA, the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the Gulf. The scheme is a 
welfare measure to support women of Indian origin in distress, through the mobilization 
of the local Indian community in the endeavour and with some financial assistance from 
the Government. 
Scope of and Eligibility for the Scheme: 
The scheme would be available to the wo men who have been deserted by their 
overseas Indian spouses or are facing divorce proceedings in a foreign country subject 
to the following conditions: 
(i)     The woman is an Indian passport holder. 
(ii)      The marriage of the woman has been solemnized in India. 
(iii)     The woman is deserted in India or after reaching abroad within five years 
of the marriage. 
(iv)     Divorce proceedings are initiated within five years of the marriage by her 
overseas Indian spouse. 
(v)   An ex- parte divorce has been ob tained by the overseas Indian spouse 
within ten years of the marriage and a case for maintenance and alimony 
is to be filed. 
(vi)    The scheme would not be available to a woman facing criminal charges or 
having a criminal case decided against her. 
(vii)    The domicile of the woman seeking relief under the scheme is not relevant 
for allowing the benefit. The woman may be domiciled in the 

Written Answers to [6 SEP., 2007] Unstarred Questions   139 
country of her overseas Indian spouse or in India at the ti me of making 
the application. 
(viii)      Preference  may be given  to applicants on  the basis  of financial needs.  
(ix)   Assistance will be limited to meeting initial cost and incidental charges for 
documentation and filing of the case by the Indian wom en’s 
organization/NGO on the woman's behalf. 
(x)   The assistance will be limited to US $1000 per case and will be released to 
the Indian community organizations/NGO concerned to enable it to take 
steps to assist the woman in documentation and preparatory work for 
filing the case. 
(xi)   The women’s organization/NGO will make efforts to enlist community 
advocates, preferably women advocates, to extend further legal 
assistance/appearance in court etc on a pro-bono basis. 
Pattern of Assistance 
Under the schem e Indian Missions in the countries concerned would empanel 
credible Indian Women’s Organizations/ Indian Community Associations/NGOs and 
their member advocates, preferably women, to provide legal aid to the victims in 
distress and whose names have been app roved by the Ministry of Overseas Indian 
Affairs. The applications for providing legal aid received by the Missions would be 
examined by an officer designated by the Head of the Mission on case -to-case basis and 
approved by Head of Mission/Deputy Chief of the Mission. 
The applications received in the Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs will be 
examined by an internal committee consisting of a legal advisor and an officer of the 
rank of Director/Deputy Secretary and approved by Secretary. Thereafter, the Min istry 
will recommend the case to Mission concerned to provide legal aid support. The 
applicant would also be informed to approach the Mission concerned in this regard.  
Financial Grants to Embassies/High Commissions 
In the current financial year (2007 -08) t he Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs 
would initially sanction Rs. 40 lakhs each to the Indian Missions in USA, UK, Canada, 
Australia, and the Gulf subject to review next year. Thus, in the current financial year 
the budget provision for this scheme will be Rs. 3.00 crore. The expenditure incurred on 
the scheme would be debited to the following Budget Head each year.

Statement 
The salient features of the proposed NRI University

†2546.   SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: 
SHRI BHAGWATI SINGH:          
SHRI BRIJ BHUSHAN TIWARI: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government’s attention has been draw n to the recently published 
Survey Report of Association for India's Development in which 81 per cent nonresident 
Indians have conceded that no work is done without corruption in India; 
(b) whether it is a fact that they have also accepted that bribe is taken  for giving 
them passport and international permit as well as during customs clearance;

and

from all spheres of life. Several steps have been initiated to remove corruption and to 
improve functioning of Government. Important among these steps are:—

Action Plan on vigilance; and

contracting processes by the CVC.

functioning through e -Governance, issue of Citizen Charters and simplification of 
procedures and systems, w hich are aimed at eradicating corruption by improving 
transparency and accountability.

Filing of closure report by CBI 
2548. SHRI MOTIUR RAHMAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state:  
(a) the details of cases where in CBI has filed closure reports in courts during the 
last three years indicating the reasons for the same; 
(b) under which circumstances the CBI files closure reports; and 
(c) whether there is any proposal to review all such closure reports filed by the CBI 
in courts; 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC 
GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI SURESH PACHOURI): (a) and (b) In respect

scrutinizing the evidence collected during investigation and on the basis of the opinion 
of the law officers. The decision on closure reports is taken by the Courts on merit. As 
such, there is no proposal to review the closure reports.

and 2004-05, the State -wise decline in the number of people living below the poverty 
line has been estimated for the period 1993- 94 to 2004- 05. These are given in the

National Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM) on 3rd December, 2005 aiming at 
reforms driven, fast track, planned development of identified cities with focus on 
efficiency in urban infrastructure/services delivery mechanism, community participation 
and accountability of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs)/Parastatals towards their citizens. A 
sum of Rs.50,000 crore has been committed as Additional Central Assistance from 
Government of India under JNNU RM for its two Sub- Missions, namely, Urban

necessary institutional changes to augment the resources of ULBs. Besides conventional 
sources, cities should take innovative measures to supplement their

Special plan for youth of hilly areas 
†2599. SHRI SAMAN PATHAK: Will the Minister of YOUTH AFFAIRS AND 
SPORTS 'be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the projects to promote youth affairs and sports with Government;  
(b) the details thereof; and 
(c) whether Government have any special plan to encourage youth of hilly areas? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI MANI SHANKAR 
AIYAR) (SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (c) The Ministry of Youth. Affairs 
and Sports implements Plan schemes for the promotion of Youth and Sports in all parts 
of the country, including hilly areas. 
For the development of youth in the country, the main schemes implemented by the 
Ministry are:—  
(i) Nehru Yuva Kendra Sanga than (NYKS): – This is a flagship programme of 
the Ministry whose main objective is to bring about social transformation in rural 
areas by promoting and developing among youth awareness and commitment to 
the concept and values of unity in diversity; nationa l integration; community 
service; discipline and scientific temper; and providing avenues to youth to strive 
towards excellence in all spheres of activity. 
(ii) National Service Volunteers Scheme (NSVS) and Rashtriya Sadbhawana 
Yojana (RSY):– These two sch emes provide opportunities to youth all over the 
country to participate in the implementation of various developmental 
programmes at the grassroots level. 
(iii) National Service -Scheme (NSS) : – NSS is at present the only Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme of the M inistry. NSS aims at the personality and character 
development of students in schools and colleges. Activities of NSS are 
implemented through the State Governments and the operations 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

Written Answers to [6 SEP., 2007] Unstarred Questions   189 
of NSS are at the University/College and Higher Secondary School level. The 
objective of the NSS is to arouse in social conscience of students and provide 
them the opportunity of working with village people and slum dwellers. 
(iv) Youth Hostels: – Youth Hostels are intended to provide low -cost budget 
accommodation to travelling youth groups to know more about the country and 
its diversity in people and culture. 
(v) Schemes for financial assistance are implemented b y the Ministry for the 
following activities:– 
(a) Promotion of adventure at basic, intermediate and advance level; 
(b) Promotion of national integration including National Youth 
Festivals, National Youth Awards and lnter -state Youth Exchange 
Programmes; 
(c) Promotion of Youth Activities and Training in the sphere of 
vocational training, entrepreneurship development and the 
organization of exhibitions; and 
(d) Development and Empowerment of Adolescents including life -
skills, education, residential camps etc. 
Likewise, for the development of sports in the country, the Ministry implements 
the following schemes through SAI:—  
(i) All India Rural Sports Tournament:–  The scheme of Rural Sports Programme 
was launched. in the year 1970 -71 with a view to broad basing games and sports  
and to tap the hidden talent in rural areas. The scheme is being operated through 
SAI. 
(ii) National Sports Festival for Women:–  The scheme of National Sports 
Festival for Women aims at arousing sports consciousness among women in the 
country. It is organized annually by the Government of India. 
(iii) Scheme for Promotion of Sports and Games in Schools: – This scheme is 
under operation since 1986. It was reviewed in 1992 with a view to raise the 
standard of sports at school -level and to encourage participat ion in inter -school 
competitions. 
(iv) Sports Scholarships Scheme: – This scheme was started to recognize the 
achievements of young sports persons and their outstanding performance at the 
National, State, College and University levels. The sports discipline s covered 
under this scheme under the category of ‘priority sports’ are Archery, Athletics, 
Badminton, Basketball, Boxing, Cycling, Football, Gymnastics, Handball, 
Hockey, Judo, Kabaddi, Kho- Kho, Rowing, Shooting, Tennis, Swimming, Table 
Tennis, Volleyball, Weightlifting and Wrestling. 
Under the category of ‘other disciplines’, are Ball Badminton, Baseball, 
Billiards and Snooker, Bowling, Carrom, Chess, Cricket, Equestrian, Fencing, 
Golf, Kayaking and Canoeing, Karate, Powerlifting, Softball, Squash, 
Taekwondo, Wushu and Yatching.

As per norms, at least 75% of the total scholarships are to be awarded to the 
priority disciplines. 
(v) North-East Sports Festival:–  The scheme of North -East Sports Festiv al was 
launched by the Department of Youth Affairs and Sports in the year 1986 -87 and 
is being operated through the SAI. 
(vi) Other main Schemes relating to the promotion of Sports activities include 
cash awards and Pension to Meritorious Sportspersons; Na tional Sports 
Development Fund; National Sports Awards Schemes; and State Sports 
Academy Scheme. 
(vii) Development of sports activities in the country is also catered through 
financial assistance to National Sports Federations by way of conducting 
national and international tournaments in India, participation of Indian Teams in 
tournaments and events abroad, provision of coaching through Indian and 
foreign coaches, backed -up with requisite technical support, procurement of 
equipments etc. 
Under the ‘Panchayat Yuva Khel aur Krida Abhiyan’, which has received 
in principle approval of the Planning Commission and is being processed further, 
special attention will be paid to sports infrastructure and organized sports in all 
parts of the country, taking into consi deration the special human endowments 
and geographical features of hill areas. The issue has also been addressed in the 
draft Comprehensive National Sports Policy, at present under discussion with 
stakeholders.

Discontinuation of assistance by Centre 
†2601. SHRI LAXMINARAYAN SHARMA: Will the Minister of YOUTH 
AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the C entral assistance for constructing sports infrastructure,  
discontinued by Central Government, is likely to be resumed; and . 
(b) if not, whether States would be provided with separate funds for this purpose?  
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI M ANI SHANKAR 
AIYAR): (a) and (b) The Centrally Sponsored Sports Infrastructure Schemes were 
transferred to the State sector w.e.f. l.4.2005. The Ministry took up, the matter with the 
Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance for reviewing the decision in view of the 
financial constraints of States. The cost -intensive nature of certain categories of 
infrastructure such as synthetic surfaces etc; and the committed liability towards the 
already approved projects. The Planning Commission did not agree to the r equest 
stating that these schemes have been identified for transfer to States as part of the 
general exercise to reduce the number of Centrally Sponsored Schemes, but agreed to 
provide funds for the completion of ongoing projects during the Tenth Plan to t he extent 
of the committed liability. 
During the current financial year 2007 -08, no funds have been provided under the 
erstwhile Sports Infrastructure Scheme. State Governments will have to fund the 
ongoing projects out of their own resources for which the y can seek additional 
allocation of funds from the Planning Commission in their respective State Annual 
Plans. 
With a view to addressing the huge gap in the availability of sports infrastructure, 
especially at the grassroots level, the Ministry have received the in-principle approval of 
the Planning Commission to launch a nation- wide programme entitled ‘‘Panchayat 
Yuva Krida Aur Khel Abhiyan’’, which aims to provide all the village and block 
panchayats with basic sports infrastructure in a phased manner over a period of 10 
years. 
The draft Comprehensive National Sports Policy also addresses this question under 
the rubric of ‘‘Sports for All’’, which is one of the objectives of the Revised Twenty -
Point Programme issued on Gandhi Jayanti 2006.

to SAI or requisition the services of these coaches on a deputation basis.  Accordingly,

P.S.Us 
SHRI MOINUL HASSAN (West Bengal): Sir, a proposal is reportedly initiated by the 
Ministry of Commerce and Industry to permit 50 per cent FDI in Defence PSUs as per 
the recommendations of the Kelkar Committee which was formed during the NDA 
regime. The Kelkar Committee’s major objective is to give open access to foreign and 
private capital in the strategic sector of defence production. It is a matter of grave 
concern that the Government, in spite of the strong opposition against the 
corporatisation of ordnance factories by various central trade unions like CITU. Defence 
Employees’ Federations, DPSU unions, is going ahead with this proposal. It is a matter 
of serious security threat to the country if assets, which are created for building 
sophisticated technology-intensive defence weapons, go to the foreign hand in the name 
of ‘‘technology’’ and ‘‘investment’’. It clearly shows that it is not the defence requirement 
but the lure for arms export business which is being eyed by such defence MNCs. Such 
arms export business by MNCs, with cheap Indian labour and ready -made infrastructure 
of Defence PSUs, is contrary to the national interest and it would never be allowed by 
the partriotic people of India. Hence, I urge upon the Government to reject the proposal 
to permit FDI in Defence PSUs and scrap the Kelkar Committee recommendation 
pertaining to ordnance factories and Defence PSUs.

Concern over suicides by farmers in Maharashtra 
SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI (Maharashtra): Sir, suicides by farmers continue 
to be a matter of serious concern to the nation as a whole. W hat happened to the 
package announced by the Prime Minister and why the assistance did not reach the 
farmers is intriguing even to the specialist enquiry committees appointed by the Prime 
Minister’s Office as also by the president of the Congress Party in the Maharashtra 
State. 
Non-performing assets amounting to Rs. 500 crores towards loans given for payment 
of interest on sugar plagued the Maharashtra State Land Development Bank. Since the 
bank went into liquidation, the only source of long-term loans for the small and marginal 
farmers dried up; this contributed substantially to the number of farmers driven to 
suicide. It was in this background that the Prime Minister had asked the Government of 
Maharashtra to present a statement on the measures taken to check the spate of 
suicides. 
The Government of Maharashtra has informed the Prime Minister’s Office that a sum 
of Rs. 600 crores was given to NABARD as soft loan towards one-time settlement. 
However, the amount has been given at a high rate of interest of 12 to 14 per cent. Since 
NABARD gives credit to the land development banks at the rate of 9.5 per cent, it is clear 
that the credit provided by the Governmert of Maharashtra would actually worsen the 
situation and increase the tendency among the farmers to desperately take recourse to 
suicides. The Government may kindly look into the matter. 
Need to control dropout rate among SC/ST students in the country 
SHRI M.V. MYSURA REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I would 
like to draw the attention of the House towards the problem of dropout among Scheduled 
Caste and Scheduled Tribe students in our country. According to a recent report, dropout 
rate among SC and ST students is going up faster than that of the general category 
students. The gap in gross dropout rate between the general category students and 
SC/ST students which was 6.7 per cent and 15.1 per cent in 2001-02 respectively went 
up to 10.4 per cent and 16.6 per cent in 2003-04. This trend is continuously increasing in 
rural areas. 
Sir, it is o bserved that there are several deficiencies and shortcomings such as poor 
utilisation of funds, non- distribution of free textbooks and uniform, lack of mid day meals, 
non-availing of schemes and programmes for these reserved categories students by the 
various States and delay in releasing of funds by the Central Government. There are no 
basic infrastructure facilities in hostels set up for SC/ST students. In Andhra Pradesh, 
several hostels which have been checked, there were no proper toilet and water supply. 
According to a Press report, huge funds were released for Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat 
and Maharashtra for the welfare of SC/ST students, but it is a matter of grave concern 
that none of the States have utilised those funds given by the Central Government, w hile 
18 other States did not get any single penny from the Central Government during the 
period 2001-06. This is a very serious matter and the Government should take effective 
measures for implementation of welfare schemes

Central Government to review the schemes formulated and to spread the light of 
education among SC/ST communities by providing basic incentives and facilities. Thank 
you, Sir. 
Demand to make necessary amendments to the medical council of India Act 
PROF. P.J. KURIEN (Kerala): Medical Council of India is approving the MBBS 
degree of the students studied in Chinese Universities after a screening test which 
comprises of three written papers based on a condensed syllabus. Nearly 10,000 
average middle-class family students have gone to China for studying MBBS course as, 
in China, the cost of studying the MBBS course is low and affordable compared to India 
and also the sam e curriculum of Medical Council of India is adopted in Chinese 
Universities. The cost of study of MBBS course in China is Rs.8 lakhs for four -and-a-half 
years including fee, food and accommodation. Their ultimate aim is to practise in India 
after study abr oad and they are better acquainted with the common diseases and 
treatments in India. So, it is unfair to show disparity towards them by enforcing a 
screening test when they studied their course in a curriculum which is the same as that 
of India. 
Considering the above facts. I would request the Government to make necessary 
amendments to the Medical Council of India Act so that they are permitted to do their 
internship in Indian colleges and hospitals. Also, the medical degree from China be 
made equivalent to Indian degree and those with MBBS degree from China may be 
given registration in the Indian Medical Council without a screening test.

Concern over global warming 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA (Chhattisgarh): Weather forecasting is a high-risk profession. 
Global Warming is not science fiction any more but a looming reality. The United 
Nation’s Inter-Governmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has predicted that 
temperatures will rise by 4 degrees by the end of the century. Climate change 

Special [6 SEP., 2007] Mentions   205 
is caused by a variety of factors but our thirst for fossil fuels is at the heart of the crisis. 
India will be one of the worst affected by climate change. According to the UN report, In 
the Himalayas, rapidly melting glaciers will cause floods followed by a dip in river flow. 
The decrease could see the Gangetic plains turn !nfertile. Cholera and malaria woul d 
increase because of floods. Cereal yields in South Asia could drop by 30 per cent by 
2050, devastating an agriculture-led rural economy like India. Food insecurity and loss of 
livelihood along with cultivable land is a nightmarish scenario. India’s vast coastline 
means flooding from rising sea levels could inundate thickly populated areas. It will also 
lead to salination of ground water. There is the threat of a shrinkage of grasslands which 
has serious implications for India which has the world’s largest cattle population. Over 25 
per cent of our plant and animal species will face extinction. Unfortunately, India has a 
dismal record on this front preferring to point fingers at countries like the US rather than 
focussing on what it should be doing. It is a  timely warning. Now, there is very little time 
to tackle a global problem in which all countries have to cooperate. If we can reverse the 
trend or even slow it down, that will be the most precious gift for the generation to follow. 
Need to stop manual scavenging in the country 
SHRIMATI N. P. DURGA (Andhra Pradesh): Shameful, disgraceful, degrading, 
dehumanizing, disgusting, obnoxious, abhorrent, a blot on humanity, are some of the 
words which can be used to describe manual scavenging. Over the years, we have set 
up Committees and Commissions, enacted laws and spent hundreds of crores to 
eradicate manual scavenging, but in vain. Even after 60 years of Independence, nothing 
has been changed. As per Safai Karrnachari Association, India has 13 lakh scavengers 
and 1.25 lakh dry latrines in 21 States and UTs. They are living In a pathetic situation; 
62% have respiratory diseases; 32% have skin diseases, 42% suffer from Hepatitis, 23%

SHRI T.R. BAALU: Sir, India has ratified the international convention SOLAS, 1974 
on 16 June, 1976 which came into force on 25 May, 1980. This Convention has been 
amended from time to time to incorporate provisions pertaining to safety of ships. During 
the Diplomatic Conference on Maritime Security held in December, 2002, amendments 
to the SOLAS 1974 were adopted including the adoption of the International Ship and 
Port Facility Security Code (ISPS). 
The objectives of the ISPS Code are 
(a) to e stablish an international framework involving cooperation between 
contracting Governments, Government agencies and shipping and port 
industries to detect security threats and take preventive measures against 
security incidents affecting ships or port facilities used in international trade; 
(b) to establish the respective roles and responsibilities of the Government, 
Government agencies, local administration and the shipping and port 
industries at the national and international level for ensuring maritime 
security; 
(c) to ensure early and efficient collection and exchange of security -related 
information; 
(d) to provide a methodology for security assessments so as to have in place 
plans and procedures to react to changing security levels; and 
(e) to ensure confidence that adequate and proportionate maritime security 
measures are in place. 
The ISPS Code will bring about uniformity in addressing security related issues of 
onboard ships and the ports in our country. The Code envisages three security levels 
commencing from level 1 to the highest level, that is, level 3. Each level shall require 
additional measures to heighten the security of ports/ships. Each ship and port will be 
guided by an approved Ship Security Plan/Port Facility Security Plan. 
In order to give effect to the provisions of the SOLAS 1974, each contracting 
Government is required to promulgate laws, decrees, orders and regulations, as 
considered necessary, so as to give full and complete effect to the Convention. This is 
with a view to ensure that ships and ports are fit for the service for which they are 
intended. 
The Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004 was originally introduced in the Lok 
Sabha on 23rd December, 2004. The Bill was referred to the Department -related 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transpo rt, Tourism and Culture for examination 
and report. The Report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee was presented to both 
Houses of Parliament on 27th July, 2005.

WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS 
Clinical trials without authorization 
*341. SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAl: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that clinical trials of drugs are being conducted 
by foreign multinationals on Indians without au thorization from the patients and 
authorities; 
(b) whether Government are also aware that these trials are being conducted without 
any clinical design; 
(c) if so, whether Government have conducted any study to find out in the past three 
years how many new drugs or  formulations have been tried on Indians by foreign drug 
companies and what has been its repercussions on the health of people; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMAN1 
RAMADOSS): (a) to (d) Government is net aware of any Global clinical trials being 
conducted by foreign multi -nationals on Indians without the permission of the Office of 
the Drugs Controller General of India {DCG(I)}. The permission to conduct any clinical 
trial with new drug in the country is a statutory requirement under Rule 122DA of Drugs 
and Cosmetics Rules, 1945. 
Clinical Trials are an integral part of clinical and drug discovery research. The 
objective of clinical research and clinical trials in human beings is to establish safety and 
efficacy of molecules that promise therapeutic benefit for various diseases and disorders 
of human beings. The global regulatory agencies also insist for trials to be conducted for 
the new drugs on multi -ethnic population of th e world to understand safety and efficacy 
issues due to ethnic variations. 
Schedule-Y of D and C Act prescribes the requirements for conducting clinical trials 
in the country and data to be furnished for conducting clinical trials. Compliance to 
Good Clinical Fractices is an important requirement of Schedule-Y. 

Written Answers to [7 SEP., 2007] Starred Questions       3 
Schedule-Y permits clinical trials for molecules discovered outside India and such 
clinical trials can be carried out by "multi -national p harmaceutical companies, local 
companies, global Clinical Research Organizations (CROs) and local CROs. For drugs 
discovered outside India, the concomitant clinical trails are permitted for Phase -II. 
Phase-III and Phase -IV and repeat Phase- I clinical trials are permitted to be conducted 
in India. The requirements specified under GCP and Schedule -Y have enough 
provisions to take care of ethical issues and safety of the subjects undergoing clinical 
trials. 
The applicant for global clinical trials has to furnish detailed information with 
respect to objective of the study, participating countries, number of patients to be 
enrolled, approvals of institutional Review Board (Ethical Committee), details of serious 
adverse reactions reported, an affidavit indicating that the studies are not discontinued, 
safety data, animal pharmacology data, data of the previous Phases of clinical trials etc. 
for examination. After examination on the matter, an NOC is granted for conducting a 
trial with specific instructions about re quirements of approval of ethical committee 
before starting of trial. 
 
As per the requirements of Schedule -Y any unexpected serious adverse event (SAE) 
occurring during a clinical trial should be communicated by the investigator to the 
sponsor within 24 hours, by the investigator to the ethics committee within 7 working 
days, and by the Sponsor to the Licensing Authority and to the other Investigator( s) 
participating in the study within 14 calendar days. 
During the past 3 years, 389 proposals for global Cl inical trials were received. No 
serious adverse events have been reported so far. 
Keeping in view the increase in the global and local clinical trials, the Government 
has made a provision in the Bill for amendment of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, 
for creation of Central Drug Authority of India, recently introduced in the Rajya Sabha, 
by incorporating a clause for punishment for violation in conducting of clinical trials 
which provides for an imprisonment of 5 years and a fine up to Rs. 10 lakhs for fir st 
offence and for subsequent offences imprisonment of 10 years and a fine of Rs. 20 
lakhs. The Bill has now been referred to the Parliamentary Standing Committee.

*345. PROF. P. J. KURIEN: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state:

set up a new railway zone in the South;

Increasing the production of ethanol 
†*347. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: 
SHRI DATTA MEGHE: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to declare some concessions for increasing the  
production of ethanol keeping in view of its utility; 
(b) whether those sugar mills which have their own distilleries but not having the 
facility of producing ethanol would be provided with concessional loans from the Sugar 
Development Fund and be allowed to set up plants; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) The Government has decided to 
encourage production and use of ethanol for blending with petrol as a fuel. Some of the 
difficulties faced by the industry in production and unrestricted movement of ethanol 
have been brought to the notice of the Government. The Government has not taken any 
final view in the matter. 
(b) and (c) The Sugar Development Fund Act and Rules were modif ied in June, 2002 
and January, 2003 respectively under which loans from Sugar Development Fund (SDF) 
are given to sugar mills for production of ethanol at a concessional rate of interest of 2% 
below the Bank Rate which effectively works out to 4% per annum  at present. Loans are 
already being provided from SDF to sugar mills which have their own distilleries for 
production of anhydrous alcohol or ethanol from alcohol as follows : 
(i)       In case any sugar factory, implementing a project for production of 
anhydrous alcohol or ethanol from alcohol, has been approved for

(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the funds eannarked for the purpose; and 
(d) whether the States would be required to share the expenditure with the Centre on 
this programme and if so, to what extent? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) to (d) Outbreak of diseases especially, water -borne and vector-borne 
diseases may occur after floods. Cholera, viral hepatitis, enteric fever and acute 
diarrhoeal diseases are the main water borne diseases caused by contamination of water 
with virus and bacteria, whereas diseases caused by, mosquitoes, which mainly breed in 
water, are dengue, malaria, filariasis, viral encephalitis etc. 
Health is a State subject and primarily, the State Government is responsible for the 
management of waterborne and other diseases in wake of the floods. The Government of 
India supplements the efforts of the State Governments/Unio n Territories by providing 
technical support and material supplies to the State Governments on their request or 
when the extent of the outbreak is beyond the coping abilities of the State. Prior to the 
onset of monsoon season, guidelines and the action req uired to be taken by the State 
Governments for prevention and control of various diseases, which may arise due to 
floods, are circulated to all the States. These guidelines elaborate on likely public health 
risks, stepping up of surveillance to detect earl y warning signs, ensuring safe drinking 
water and instituting Public health measures to prevent outbreak of diseases. 
The Government of India provides financial assistance to the States affected by 
natural calamities as per norms of Calamity Relief Fund (C RF) shared by the Centre and 
the State on 75:25 basis. If the calamity is of severe nature, additional funds are also 
made available from National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF). The 

12     Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Starred Questions 
requirement of the additional funds is assessed by Ministry of Home Affairs, which is 
the nodal Ministry for the fund. The CRF and NCCF norms include assistance for 
provision of medicines, disinfectants, insecticides for prevention and outbreak of 
epidemics. 
In addi tion, a comprehensive National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme 
(NVBDCP) is implemented through the States for prevention and control of vector 
borne diseases caused by mosquitoes. The strategies for control of vector borne diseases 
include disease m anagement through early case detection and, treatment, epidemic 
preparedness and rapid response. An integrated approach has been initiated with 
Department of Drinking Water Supply to provide the technical support to monitor the 
quality of drinking water in  different States so as to prevent occurrence of water borne 
diseases. 
The Government of India has also launched an Integrated Disease Surveillance 
Programme in November, 2004, to further strengthen identification of outbreaks of 
various diseases including water borne and vector borne diseases so that early 
intervention could be made and occurrence, disability and death due to such diseases 
could be reduced.

*354.   SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: 
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether as per a report called Towards Universal Access: Scaling Up Priority  
HIV/AIDS Intervent ions in the Health Sector, jointly released by the World Health  
Organisation (WHO), UNAIDS and UNICEF recently states that among the 39.5  
million people living with HIV/AIDS in the world, 5.7 millions are in India; 
(b) whether the National AIDS Control Org anisation started giving free  
paediatric doses of anti -retroviral drugs to children under the national programme  
in December 2006; and 
(c) the steps Government propose to take to provide treatment to all the HIV  
and AIDS patients free of cost? 
THE MINISTER  OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) to (c) In its report on the Global AIDS epidemic published by 
UNAIDS in May, 2006, 5.7million persons were estimated to be living with HIV/AIDS 
in India During 2007, NACO reviewed the estimation me thod alongwith national and 
international experts; including UNAIDS, WHO, CDC Atlanta etc. The review was 
carried out keeping in mind the availability of reports based on National Family Health 
Survey-III, Integrated Biological and Behaviour Survey in High Risk Groups and an 
expanded sentinel surveillance. Following the expert consultation, NACO estimated that 
persons living with HIV/AIDS in India range between 2 to 3 million. Of them, it is 
estimated that there are 70,000 children below 15 years of age who  are living with the 
virus. 
In order to ensure universal access of treatment to children, the National Peadiatric 
AIDS initiative was launched on 30th November, 2006. Under this Initiative, free 
paediatric doses of Anti-retroviral (ARV) drugs and free diagnostics 

Written Answers to [7 SEP., 2007] Starred Questions     19 
are provided. Special campaigns were launched to screen high risk children so as to 
detect and treat HIV infected children. Till date, 22,217 new HIV+ children have been 
detected and 6338 children eligible put on ART at 127 ART centres in 31 States of the 
country. The peadiatric formulations of ARVs for 17,000 children have been made 
available at these centres. This initiative also includes developing paediatric ART 
guidelines, training of pediatricians and counselors, establishment of seven Regional 
Paediatric ART centres, free CD4 monitoring, free DNA PCR test for children up to 18 
months, liquid formulations for babies weighing less than 5 kg, diagnosis and treatment 
of opportunistic infections and micro-nutrient supplementation. 
Under NACP-III, it is proposed to provide free ART to 300,000 adults and 40,000 
children through 250 ART Centres and Link ART Centres. All HIV positive persons 
accessing public health facilities and clinically eli gible for ART shall be provided free 
ART.

Rising cases of polio 
*357.   SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether rising polio cases continue to depict the country in a poor light as it 
stands above Pakistan and Afghanistan and next to Nigeria in the total number of polio 
cases reported worldwide in 2007; 
(b) if so, whethe r Government had asked ICMR to carry out research studies 
alongwith the State Governments to work out strategy for effectively tackle the rising 
cases; 
(c) if so, whether ICMR has already submitted its report and suggested the strategy 
for future polio campaigns in the country; and 
(d) if so, what are the steps being considered to implement the suggestions made?  
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) The annual strategy for polio eradication is decided on the basis of 
the recommendat ion of the Indian Expert Advisory Group (IEAG) consisting of 
National experts and International experts from World Health Organization (WHO), 
United Nation's Children Fund (UNICEF), Centre for Diseases Control (CDC) Atlanta. 
The IEAG reviews the polio epid emiological situation two times a year and recommend 
the suitable strategies for the country. The National Polio Surveillance Project (NPSP) 
of WHO provides technical support for high quality Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) 
surveillance and assists the Gover nment in microplanning, training and monitoring of 
polio immunization campaign. 
During this year, so far 185 polio cases have been reported in the country, out of 
which 49 are of Polio Type 1 and 136 are of Polio Type 3. There has been significant 
decline in the number of cases caused by the most virulent strain of poliovirus type 1 (P 
1 ). The endemic region of western Uttar Pradesh has reported - only three type 1 polio 
cases this year. The core districts of Moradabad and J P Nagar, the epicenter of the 
outbreak last year, have not had a single case of P 1 for the last 8 months. 

24     V/ritten Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Starred Questions 
The number of cases caused by the other surviving strain of Poliovirus Type 3, (P3) 
has risen this year to 136, but the c irculation is confined to limited geographical area of 
Western Uttar Pradesh and Udham Singh Nagar district of Uttarakhand . This rise is 
consistent with the immunization strategy recommended by the 1EAG focusing on Polio 
Type 1 virus through the use of mo re efficacious monovalent type 1 polio vaccine since 
April, 2005. The immunization strategy has been focusing on curtailing Polio Type 1 
virus and keeping Polio Type 3 virus in check because PI circulates more widely, has 
been responsible for international spread and has the propensity to cause large outbreaks. 
Similar trend of rise in Polio Type 3 cases and decline in Polio Type 1 cases is also seen 
in Nigeria, Pakisthan and Afganistan this year. 
The number of polio cases by Type detected in India, Pakistan, Afganistan and 
Nigeria during this year is enclosed as Statement (See below). 
(b) to (d) The ICMR is working closely with the Government of Uttar Pradesh and 
National Polio Surveillance Project to work out strategies for polio eradication in UP. 
Several rounds of OPV vaccination campaigns have been carried out in UP in 2006 and 
2007. Understanding the level of immunity in areas where immunity gaps persisted 
despite vaccination campaigns is crucial to the success of polio eradication in UP.  
Entrovirus Research Centre of ICMR has been closely analyzing the available data in 
collaboration with NPSP and other experts. ICMR has taken up two studies to evaluate 
populations immunity (to understand immunity gaps) 
(1) determine  prevalence of poliovirus  antibodies  in  normal  healthy children 
in Moradabad district and

(c) whether it is also a fact that the production of pulses and oilseeds in the country
